questions.why: After a modal verb we use be + the past participle, so must repair becomes must be repaired.

questions.q: Rewrite in the passive: *Scientists have discovered a new medicine.*
options: A new medicine has been discovered by scientists.
A new medicine have been discovered by scientists.
A new medicine has discovered by scientists.
A new medicine was been discovered by scientists.
questions.topic: Passive in the present perfect: has/have been + past participle
questions.lesson: Passive forms - تكوين المبني للمجهول وخطوات التحويل
questions.why: The present perfect passive is has/have been + past participle, and the new singular subject takes has.

Language review 5 › Expressing quantity.lesson: Expressing quantity | التعبير عن الكمية (too much / too many - less / fewer)

questions.q: Which of these nouns is uncountable?
questions.topic: Uncountable nouns
questions.lesson: Expressing quantity | التعبير عن الكمية (too much / too many - less / fewer)
questions.why: Advice cannot be counted and has no plural form; we say 'some advice', not 'two advices' — like water and rice in the lesson.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *You shouldn't spend too ____ time playing video games every evening.*
questions.topic: too much + uncountable nouns
questions.lesson: Expressing quantity | التعبير عن الكمية (too much / too many - less / fewer)
questions.why: 'Time' is uncountable, so it takes 'too much': too much time.

questions.q: Complete the question: *How ____ sugar do you take in your tea?*
questions.topic: much / many in questions
questions.lesson: Expressing quantity | التعبير عن الكمية (too much / too many - less / fewer)
questions.why: 'Sugar' is uncountable, so we ask 'How much sugar?'; 'How many' is used only with countable plural nouns.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *There are only ____ chairs in the room, so two students will stand.*
questions.topic: a few with countable plural nouns
questions.lesson: Expressing quantity | التعبير عن الكمية (too much / too many - less / fewer)
questions.why: 'Chairs' is a countable plural noun, so we use 'a few'; 'a little' is used only with uncountable nouns.

questions.q: What does the word 'too' add to the meaning of 'much' or 'many' in a sentence like 'He eats too much rice'?
options: It shows that the amount is more than he needs.
It asks about the amount of something.
It shows that the amount is enough for him.
It shows the exact number of things.
questions.topic: the negative meaning of 'too'

questions.lesson: Passive forms - المبني للمجهول في جميع الأزمنة والأفعال الناقصة

questions.q: What is the difference in meaning between *The window was broken* and *The window has been broken*?

questions.why: "Letters" is plural, so the past simple passive needs "were", not "was".

questions.why: The continuous passive adds 'being' to be, and 'right now' shows a continuous action: is being repaired.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *Three students ____ injured in the accident so far.*

The final match is played in Cairo.

questions.lesson: Passive forms - المبني للمجهول في جميع الأزمنة والأفعال الناقصة
questions.why: After 'will' the passive adds 'be' + past participle: will be played.

questions.q: Change the direct order into a polite request with 'Would you mind': *Turn down the music!*

Would you mind turn down the music?
Would you mind to turn down the music?
Would you mind turned down the music?
questions.topic: Changing an order into Would you mind + -ing

questions.why: 'Would you mind' must be followed by the -ing form: 'Would you mind turning down the music?'

questions.q: Complete the dialogue with the correct polite request: *A: ____ B: Certainly. Here you are.*

May I borrowing your ruler, please?
May I to borrow your ruler, please?
Would you mind borrow your ruler, please?
questions.topic: Choosing the request that matches 'Certainly. Here you are.'
questions.lesson: Making polite requests | تقديم الطلبات بأدب
questions.why: 'May I borrow ...?' asks for something for yourself, and 'Certainly. Here you are.' is a suitable agreeing reply.

questions.q: Complete with the correct form: *Could you ____ me move this table, please?* (help)
questions.topic: 'Could you' + base verb without 'to'
questions.lesson: Making polite requests | تقديم الطلبات بأدب
questions.why: After 'Could you' we use the base verb with no 'to', so the lesson marks 'Could you to carry this?' as wrong.

questions.q: Choose the reply that gives permission: *May I borrow your ruler for a moment?*
questions.topic: Reply to 'May I ...?'
questions.lesson: Making polite requests | تقديم الطلبات بأدب
questions.why: The lesson answers 'May I ...?' with 'Certainly.' (or 'Of course.'), as in 'May I use your pen? - Of course.'

questions.q: Read the dialogue. A: *Would you mind waiting for a few minutes?* B: *Yes.* What does B mean?

B wants A to wait for him.
B did not hear the question.

questions.q: Your classmate says: *Could you lend me your bicycle for the weekend?* You are using it yourself, so you cannot lend it. Which is the best answer?

questions.topic: Polite refusal of a request
questions.lesson: Making polite requests | تقديم الطلبات بأدب
questions.why: The lesson refuses politely with 'I'm sorry, ...', as in 'I'm sorry, I need it today.'

questions.q: Choose the two correct replies. A: *Would you mind lending me your notes for tonight?* B: ____ A: *Could you show me the way to the post office?* B: ____
options: Not at all. / Yes, I do.

questions.q: Your teacher says: *Would you mind not using your phone in the lesson?* What does she want you to do?

questions.topic: Meaning of 'Would you mind not + -ing'

Language review 2 › Saying where things.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية

questions.q: What is a prepositional phrase of place made of?
options: A preposition + a noun, e.g. *in the corner*
A verb + an adverb, e.g. *sit down*
An adjective + a noun, e.g. *small room*
questions.topic: Structure of a prepositional phrase
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson says a prepositional phrase is a preposition + a noun, e.g. in the corner, next to the armchair.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: *There ____ two armchairs and a sofa in the living room.*
questions.topic: There is / There are with plural nouns
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson says we use There's for one thing and There are for more than one, and two armchairs and a sofa are plural.

questions.q: Complete: *The ladder is ____ the wall so that it does not fall down.*
questions.topic: against the wall (leaning)
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson gives against = leaning on / supported by the wall, as in There's a bookcase against the wall.

questions.q: Complete: *There's a fridge ____ the corner of the kitchen.*
questions.topic: in the corner of a room
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson says in the corner is used for the inside corner of a room, while at the corner is for the corner of a street.

questions.q: Complete the sentence to mean 'on the right side of the door specifically': *There's a map ____ the door.*
questions.topic: to the right of + noun vs on the right
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson says to the right of needs of + the thing (to the left of the window), while on the right is used on its own.

questions.q: The pharmacy and the hospital share the same wall. Complete: *The pharmacy is ____ the hospital.*
questions.topic: next to (side by side) vs near
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson says next to means directly beside, but near only means close by, not necessarily touching.

questions.q: You have to cross the road to get from the bank to the café. Complete: *The café is ____ the bank.*
questions.topic: opposite (across a space) vs in front of
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson says opposite means in the facing position with a space between, while in front of is close and face to face.

questions.q: Which sentence has a mistake?
options: *There's a rug in the middle of the room.*
*There's a lamp on the small table.*
questions.topic: on the wall vs in the wall
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The lesson says on the wall is for something hanging, like a picture, so in the wall is wrong; the other three phrases are used correctly.

questions.q: Read: *There's a wardrobe against the wall on the left of the bedroom. There's a chest of drawers next to the wardrobe, and a mirror above the chest of drawers. The bed is opposite the wardrobe.* Where would you see the mirror?
options: Above the chest of drawers, next to the wardrobe
Above the bed, opposite the wardrobe
Against the wall, opposite the chest of drawers
In the middle of the bedroom, above the bed
questions.topic: Inferring the position of an object from a description
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The description puts the chest of drawers next to the wardrobe and the mirror above the chest of drawers, so the mirror is above it.

questions.q: Join the two sentences in one sentence with *between ... and ...*: *The baker's is on one side of the bank. The chemist's is on the other side of the bank.*
options: The bank is between the baker's and the chemist's.
The bank is in the middle of the baker's and the chemist's.
The baker's is between the bank and the chemist's.
The chemist's is between the baker's and the bank.
questions.topic: Joining two sentences with between ... and ...
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The bank is the thing in the middle, so the pattern is: the bank + is between + the baker's + and + the chemist's.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *There is a lamp ____ the bed.*
questions.topic: The phrase 'next to'
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: 'Next' must be followed by 'to': 'next to the bed', as the lesson shows with 'next to the armchair'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *There is a table in the middle ____ the kitchen.*
questions.topic: 'of' in 'in the middle of'
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: 'In the middle of' always takes 'of'; 'in the middle the room' is a mistake the lesson warns about.

questions.q: One of these sentences has a mistake. Which one? *There is a clock on the wall above the door.* / *There is a fridge in the middle of the kitchen.* / *There is a mirror in front the door.* / *There is a lamp between the bed and the window.*
options: There is a clock on the wall above the door.
There is a fridge in the middle of the kitchen.
There is a mirror in front the door.
There is a lamp between the bed and the window.
questions.topic: 'in front of' — the missing 'of'
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: 'In front of' needs 'of'; 'in front the door' is exactly the mistake the lesson lists.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *Our school is ____ the hospital.*
questions.topic: 'opposite' without 'of'
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: 'Opposite' does not need 'of': we say 'opposite the hospital', and 'opposite of the bookcase' is wrong.

questions.q: Make one sentence from these two ideas, using *between*: *The cinema is on the left of our house. The bank is on the right of our house.*
options: Our house is between the cinema and the bank.
Our house is between the cinema or the bank.
Our house is between cinema and bank.
Our house is among the cinema and the bank.
questions.topic: Joining two places with 'between ... and'
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: 'Between' joins two places with 'and', and 'the' stays before each place.

questions.q: Read about Salem's room: *The door is on the right. The wardrobe is in the corner next to the door. The desk is opposite the bed, under the window.* Which sentence is correct?
options: The wardrobe is near the door.
The bed is under the window.
The desk is next to the door.
The door is on the left.
questions.topic: Understanding a room description
questions.lesson: Saying where things are: Prepositional phrases | وصف أماكن الأشياء بحروف الجر المكانية
questions.why: The wardrobe is next to the door, so it is near it; the desk, not the bed, is under the window.

Language review 2 › Direct and Indirect.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة

questions.q: What is an indirect question?
options: A direct question with the verb before its subject
A polite question that uses statement word order
A question that is answered only by yes or no
A question that repeats the speaker's exact words
questions.topic: Definition of an indirect question
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: An indirect question begins with a polite opening phrase and then puts the words in statement order, subject before verb.

questions.q: Which words are left out when a direct question becomes an indirect question?
questions.topic: Dropping do, does and did
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: The lesson says do, does and did are removed and the main verb takes its correct tense instead.

questions.q: Complete the indirect question: *Do you know ____ the library is open?*
questions.topic: Using if with yes/no questions
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: A yes/no question takes if (or whether) after the introductory phrase, with statement order after it.

questions.q: Which introductory phrase is used to ask politely whether someone has an idea about something?
questions.topic: The phrase 'Have you any idea'
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: 'Have you any idea …?' is listed in the lesson as the polite way of asking if someone has an idea about something.

questions.q: Change into an indirect question beginning with 'Do you know': *When does the train leave?*
options: Do you know when does the train leave?
Do you know when the train leaves?
Do you know when the train leave?
Do you know when does the train leaves?
questions.topic: Change of does to -s in indirect questions
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: With does we drop it and add -s to the main verb: does the train leave becomes the train leaves.

questions.q: Why does the verb come after the subject in *Could you tell me where the station is?*
options: Because the sentence does not have a question word
Because 'the station' is the object of the verb
Because indirect questions use statement word order
Because the sentence is in the past simple tense
questions.topic: Position of the auxiliary after the subject
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: In an indirect question the auxiliary is placed after the subject, exactly as in a normal statement.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: I'd like to know where the new office is?
Do you know where the new office is.
Can you tell me where the new office is.
I'd like to know where the new office is.
questions.topic: Punctuation of indirect questions
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: 'I'd like to know' is a statement, so the sentence ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.q: Why does the speaker use an indirect question in *Excuse me, could you tell me where the city museum is?*
options: Because he wants to give the listener an order
Because he is speaking to someone he does not know
Because he is talking to a close friend at home
Because he is answering a teacher's question
questions.topic: When to use indirect questions
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: The lesson says we use indirect questions with people we do not know, in formal situations, and to be polite.

questions.q: Rewrite as an indirect question beginning with 'Could you tell me': *Where did you buy your laptop?*
options: Could you tell me where did you buy your laptop?
Could you tell me where you buy your laptop?
Could you tell me where you bought your laptop?
Could you tell me where do you bought your laptop?
questions.topic: Two-step change with did into the past simple
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: We drop did, put the words in statement order, and the main verb becomes past simple: did you buy becomes you bought.

questions.q: Rewrite as an indirect question beginning with 'Do you know': *Have the guests arrived?*
options: Do you know if have the guests arrived?
Do you know if the guests have arrive?
Do you know if do the guests arrived?
Do you know if the guests have arrived?
questions.topic: Indirect yes/no question with have + past participle
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: A yes/no question takes if, then statement order, and the present perfect have arrived stays the same.

questions.q: What happens to the word order when a direct question is changed into an indirect question?
options: The subject moves before the verb, as in a statement.
The verb stays before the subject, as in the direct question.
The auxiliary verb moves to the end of the sentence.
The subject and the verb change places twice.
questions.topic: Word order in indirect questions
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb: Where is the market? → Can you tell me where the market is?

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *Do you know what time the film ____?* (start)
questions.topic: Dropping does and adding -s to the verb
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: When does is dropped, the verb takes -s: What time does the film start? → what time the film starts.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly changes this Yes/No question into an indirect one? *Is the library open on Friday?*
options: Do you know if the library is open on Friday?
Do you know if is the library open on Friday?
Do you know does the library open on Friday?
Do you know that the library is open on Friday?
questions.topic: Changing Yes/No questions with if
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: A Yes/No question takes if, and the subject comes before the verb: Do you know if the library is open on Friday?

questions.q: Choose the correct way to make this question polite and indirect: *Where can I find the science lab?*
options: Could you tell me where I can find the science lab?
Could you tell me where can I find the science lab?
Could you tell me where I find can the science lab?
Could you tell me where do I can find the science lab?
questions.topic: Position of modals after the subject
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: The modal can is moved after the subject: Where can I find…? → Could you tell me where I can find…?

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this sentence: *Can you tell me where is the nearest pharmacy?*
options: Can you tell me where the nearest pharmacy is?
Can you tell me where is the nearest pharmacy?
Can you tell me where does the nearest pharmacy is?
Can you tell me where the nearest pharmacy are?
questions.topic: Correcting inversion mistakes in indirect questions
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: There is no inversion in an indirect question, so is goes after the subject: where the nearest pharmacy is.

questions.q: Which indirect question is formed correctly from this direct question? *When did the match finish?*
options: Do you know when the match finished?
Do you know when did the match finish?
Do you know when the match did finish?
Do you know when did the match finished?
questions.topic: Past tense after dropping did
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: Did is dropped and the verb becomes past simple: When did the match finish? → Do you know when the match finished?

questions.q: What is true about the phrases 'Can you tell me', 'Could you tell me' and 'Do you know'?
options: Any of them can introduce the same indirect question.
Only 'Do you know' can be used with Yes/No questions.
Each of them must be followed by a different verb form.
Only 'Could you tell me' is used in polite speech.
questions.topic: Interchangeable polite openers
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: The lesson notes that Can you tell me, Could you tell me or Do you know can be used in any of these indirect questions.

questions.q: Rewrite as an indirect question beginning with 'Do you know': *Can students use dictionaries in the exam?*
options: Do you know if students can use dictionaries in the exam?
Do you know if can students use dictionaries in the exam?
Do you know that students can use dictionaries in the exam?
Do you know if students use can dictionaries in the exam?
questions.topic: Yes/No questions with a modal in indirect form
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: The Yes/No question takes if, and the modal can moves after the subject students.

questions.q: Choose the correct indirect form of: *How long has Fatima been studying medicine?*
options: Could you tell me how long Fatima has been studying medicine?
Could you tell me how long has Fatima been studying medicine?
Could you tell me how long does Fatima has been studying medicine?
Could you tell me how long Fatima been has studying medicine?
questions.topic: Auxiliary has after the subject in indirect questions
questions.lesson: Direct and Indirect questions | الأسئلة المباشرة وغير المباشرة
questions.why: The auxiliary has is moved after the subject Fatima, so no inversion remains in the indirect question.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: *Our school day starts ____ eight o'clock.*
questions.topic: at + exact clock times
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: *In many countries, the new school year begins ____ September.*
questions.topic: in + months
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: *The museum is closed ____ Sundays.*
questions.topic: on + days of the week
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: *The manager is busy ____ present, so please call back later.*
questions.topic: at + fixed expressions
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?

Our first class is in Sunday morning.
Our first class is at Sunday morning.
Our first class is for Sunday morning.
questions.topic: on + day + part of the day
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Which of these time expressions is NOT correct in English?
questions.topic: in with seasons, months and parts of the day
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct pair of prepositions: *He drinks tea ____ the morning, but he never drinks coffee ____ night.*
questions.topic: in the morning contrasted with at night
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on
questions.why: Parts of the day take in, but night is the fixed exception that takes at.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct pair of prepositions: *The first railway engines were built ____ the 19th century, and the first metro opened ____ 1973.*
questions.topic: in + centuries and years
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on
questions.why: In is used with long periods: in the 19th century and in 1973.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct pair of prepositions: *My sister was born ____ 3rd March ____ 2011.*
questions.topic: on + dates and in + years in one sentence
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence after adding the day *Friday* before the time expression: *The match begins in the afternoon.*

The match begins at Friday afternoon.
The match begins on Friday the afternoon.

questions.q: Correct the mistake: *The new term begins on next week.*

The new term begins on next week.
The new term begins next week.
The new term begins at next week.
questions.topic: no preposition before next
questions.lesson: Expressions of time with prepositions at, in and on | حروف الجر الزمنية at و in و on

questions.q: Re-order from the widest period of time to the narrowest: *season / day / clock time*

questions.q: Why do we say *on Monday morning* but *in the morning*?

Because 'prefer' must be followed by 'ones' and never by 'one'

questions.q: In the sentence *The blue notebook is mine and the red one is on the desk*, what does the word 'one' stand for?

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct word: *The tea in this cup is hotter than the ____ in that pot.*

questions.q: Why is *She bought a new one* correct, but *She bought a new* wrong?
options: Because 'one' carries the noun, and an adjective cannot replace a noun by itself
Because 'new' must change to 'newer' at the end of a sentence
Because the article 'a' must come after the adjective in English

questions.topic: Backshift of 'will' to 'would'

questions.why: Four changes happen together: 'we' → 'they', 'here' → 'there', 'will' → 'would', 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'.

questions.topic: Turning a strong disagreement into a polite partial agreement
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: *That's true, but ...* agrees partly and then gives a different opinion politely, which is what the lesson recommends.

questions.q: Correct the mistake: *My friend is not agree with the new timetable.*
options: My friend don't agree with the new timetable.
My friend isn't agree with the new timetable.
My friend doesn't agree with the new timetable.
My friend not agree with the new timetable.
questions.topic: Negative form of 'agree': 'doesn't agree'
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: The lesson corrects 'I am not agree' to 'I don't agree'; with he/she we say 'doesn't agree'.

questions.q: Correct the mistake: *In my opinion, I think homework should be shorter.*
options: In my opinion, I think homework should be shorter.
According to my opinion, I think homework should be shorter.
I think in my opinion homework should be shorter.
In my opinion, homework should be shorter.
questions.topic: Avoiding repetition of 'In my opinion' and 'I think'
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: The lesson says 'In my opinion, I think ...' repeats the same idea, so we use only one of them.

questions.q: Which reply agrees only partly with this opinion: *Living in a village is boring.*
options: That's true, but village life is peaceful and friendly.
I completely disagree with you about villages.
I am not agree with this opinion about villages.
Yes, I am agree that a village is boring.
questions.topic: 'That's true, but ...' for partial agreement
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: The lesson uses 'That's true, but ...' to accept part of the idea and then give a different view.

questions.q: Choose the strongest way to disagree with this opinion: *Sport is a waste of time.*
options: I completely disagree with that; sport keeps us healthy.
That's true, but sport is also fun.
I don't have any clear opinion about sport.
I agree that sport takes a lot of time.
questions.topic: Strong disagreement with 'I completely disagree'
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: 'I completely disagree' is the strongest expression in the lesson; 'That's true, but ...' only agrees partly.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the best reason: *I totally agree that learning English is important because ____.*
options: it helps us find better jobs in the future
this is my opinion about English
questions.topic: Supporting agreement with a reason
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: The lesson's model answers always add a real reason after agreeing, as in 'I believe tourism brings money and jobs'.

questions.q: Huda says: *"I believe fast food is good for students."* Choose the reply that disagrees AND gives a reason.
options: I completely disagree. In my opinion, it is unhealthy and expensive.
That's true, but in my opinion fast food is good for students.
I am not agree with Huda, and I think she is wrong.
According to my opinion, fast food is good for students.
questions.topic: Disagreeing with a speaker and giving a reason
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: The reply must do two things: disagree ('I completely disagree') and then give a reason ('it is unhealthy and expensive').

questions.q: Rewrite this opinion politely, using partial agreement and one reason: *Watching films is a waste of time.*
options: That's true, but in my opinion some films teach us about other cultures.
I am not agree with this opinion about films.
According to my opinion, films are a waste of time.
I completely agree that watching films is a waste of time.
questions.topic: Polite partial agreement with a reason
questions.lesson: Expressing opinions | التعبير عن الرأي والموافقة والاعتراض
questions.why: 'That's true, but ...' is the lesson's polite way to agree partly, and the reply adds a supporting reason.

Language review 4 › Useful expressions |.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية

questions.q: Choose the correct reply: *You meet your father's manager for the first time. He says, How do you do?*
questions.topic: The reply to 'How do you do?'
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: The lesson says 'How do you do?' is a formal greeting at a first meeting and the reply is the same words, not 'I'm fine'.

questions.q: Choose the best expression to complete the sentence: *Today is Rami's tenth birthday, so we say to him, ____*
questions.topic: Many happy returns — birthday greeting
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: The lesson gives 'Many happy returns (of the day)' as the expression we say on a person's birthday.

questions.q: Complete the dialogue: *My brother is starting a new job in Dubai next week. ____*
questions.topic: Best wishes for the future — occasions of use
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'Best wishes for the future' is said to someone who is beginning a new life, such as a wedding, a graduation, travel or a new job.

questions.q: Choose what you say: *You are leaving your teacher's house after a pleasant evening visit.*
questions.topic: Thank you for inviting me — leaving a visit
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: The lesson says 'Thank you for inviting me' is used when leaving a party or a visit.

questions.q: Study the two short exchanges, then choose the correct difference: *(1) Sami says, How do you do? and Nabil answers, How do you do? (2) Sami says, How are you? and Nabil answers, I'm fine, thanks.*
options: Exchange 1 is a formal greeting at a first meeting; exchange 2 asks about someone we already know.
Exchange 1 asks about someone's health; exchange 2 is used only at a first meeting.
Both exchanges are used when we meet a stranger for the first time.
Exchange 1 is answered with I'm fine, thanks; exchange 2 is answered with How do you do.
questions.topic: 'How do you do?' vs 'How are you?'
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'How do you do?' is a formal greeting on first meeting, answered by the same words, while 'How are you?' asks about a person we know.

questions.q: Choose the best expression for this situation: *Your little brother cleaned the whole kitchen while your mother was ill, and you want to praise his effort.*
questions.topic: 'Well done!' vs 'Congratulations!'
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'Well done!' focuses on the effort a person made, while 'Congratulations!' focuses on a happy occasion.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence to write on a card: *Sami has just got a new job.*
questions.topic: 'Congratulations' always ends in -s
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: The lesson notes that 'Congratulations' is always written with an -s at the end, and it takes 'on' before the occasion.

questions.q: Choose the correct pair for the two situations: *(1) ____, is this seat free? (2) ____? I didn't hear your name.*
questions.topic: 'Excuse me' vs 'Pardon?'
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'Excuse me' attracts a stranger's attention politely, while 'Pardon?' is used when you did not hear what was said.

questions.q: Rewrite this direct question as a polite request, beginning with Excuse me: *Where is the nearest hospital?*
options: Excuse me. Could you tell me where the nearest hospital is?
Excuse me. Could you tell me where is the nearest hospital?
Excuse me. Could you telling me where the nearest hospital is?
Excuse me. Could you tell me where the nearest hospital?
questions.topic: Polite indirect question with 'Could you tell me…?'
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: The lesson's model is 'Excuse me. Could you tell me where the museum is?' — after the polite opener we keep normal word order and a full verb.

questions.q: Read the situation and choose the correct pair: *On his way out of his friend's house after dinner, Omar meets his friend's father, Mr Nabil, for the first time. Omar wants to thank his friend and greet Mr Nabil politely.*
options: Thank you for inviting me. / How do you do?
Well done! / Best wishes for the future.
questions.topic: Choosing two suitable expressions in one situation
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'Thank you for inviting me' is said when leaving a visit, and 'How do you do?' is the formal greeting at a first meeting.

questions.q: Complete the sentence correctly: *Thank you for ____ me to your birthday party.*
questions.topic: -ing form after 'for' in thank-you expressions
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: After 'for' the verb takes -ing: 'Thank you for inviting me', not 'Thank you for invite me'.

questions.q: Which expression can you say in BOTH of these situations? *Your brother has just passed his driving test.* / *Your cousin has just got married.*
options: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
questions.topic: One expression used for two different occasions
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'Congratulations' is used for success and for a marriage, while 'Many happy returns' is only for a birthday.

questions.q: *Your teacher said something, but you did not hear the words clearly.* Which is the most polite thing to say?
options: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
questions.topic: Asking somebody politely to repeat
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'Sorry, could you say that again, please?' is the polite expression, while 'What?', 'Repeat!' and 'Speak up!' are rude.

questions.q: Which expression is used when somebody gets married, but NOT when somebody has a birthday?
questions.topic: Wedding wishes compared with birthday wishes
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: The lesson gives 'Best wishes for the future' for a wedding and 'Many happy returns' for a birthday.

questions.q: *I have just passed my final exam.* Which reply is both suitable and correctly written?
options: How do you do? Well done!
questions.topic: Choosing a suitable and correctly written reply
questions.lesson: Useful expressions | عبارات مفيدة في المواقف الاجتماعية
questions.why: 'Well done! Congratulations!' suits an exam success, and 'Congratulations' is written in the plural.

questions.q: What does 'make' mean in this sentence? *Warm weather makes the plants grow fast.*
options: It means 'cause' — one thing causes a result.
questions.topic: meaning of causative 'make' (cause)
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: Here 'make' means 'cause': the warm weather causes the plants to grow fast.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct verb form: *The funny story made the whole class ____.*
questions.topic: make + object + bare infinitive
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: After make + object we use the bare infinitive, so 'laugh' is correct, not 'to laugh'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct word: *The heavy rain made the roads ____.*
questions.topic: make + object + adjective
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: After make + object we can use an adjective ('dangerous') to describe the object.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: *Swimming in the sea ____ me hungry.*
questions.topic: make/makes with an -ing subject
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: An -ing subject (Swimming) is singular, so it takes 'makes'.

questions.q: In which sentence does 'make' mean 'produce or build something' rather than 'cause'?
options: The medicine made the child sleepy.
The new teacher made the class quiet.
My uncle made a wooden table for the garden.
The loud noise made the baby cry.
questions.topic: causative make vs make = produce
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: 'Made a wooden table' means produced or built it; the other three sentences mean 'caused'.

questions.q: Correct the mistake in this sentence: *The hot weather makes me to feel tired.*
options: The hot weather makes me feeling tired.
The hot weather makes me to feeling tired.
The hot weather make me feel tired.
The hot weather makes me feel tired.
questions.topic: no 'to' after make + object
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: Make + object is followed by the bare infinitive, so 'to' must be dropped.

questions.q: Why do we use 'make' and not 'makes' in this sentence? *Regular exercise and healthy food make you strong.*
options: Because the verb is in the past tense form.
Because the subject is plural — two things joined by 'and'.
Because the sentence has an adjective after it.
Because the subject is an -ing form of a verb.
questions.topic: make with a plural subject
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural, so the verb is 'make', not 'makes'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct verb form: *Last summer, the long journey ____ my grandparents very tired.*
questions.topic: past form 'made'
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: 'Last summer' shows past time, and the past form of 'make' is 'made'.

questions.q: Combine the two sentences into one sentence using 'make': *Sara heard the bad news. She cried.*
options: The bad news made her to cry.
The bad news made she cry.
The bad news made her cry.
The bad news was made her cry.
questions.topic: joining two sentences with the causative 'make'
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: Make + object + bare infinitive joins the two ideas: the bad news made her cry.

questions.q: Rewrite with 'make' so that the meaning stays the same: *Ahmed is very happy because he passed the exam.* → The exam results ____.
questions.topic: rewriting with make + object + adjective
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: The result 'happy' is an adjective, so the answer is 'made Ahmed happy'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: *A long bus ride ____ young children hungry and tired.*
questions.topic: Adjective after make + object
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: The singular subject 'A long bus ride' takes 'makes', and the adjective 'hungry' describes the object.

questions.q: Re-order the words to make a correct sentence: *sleepy / us / the mountain walk / made*
options: The mountain walk made us sleepy.
The mountain walk made us to be sleepy.
The mountain walk makes us sleepy.
The mountain walk made us sleeping.
questions.topic: Word order with make + object + adjective
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: The correct order is subject + made + object + adjective: The mountain walk made us sleepy.

questions.q: Complete both sentences: *A warm drink ____ me relaxed.* / *Warm drinks ____ me relaxed.*
questions.topic: Singular and plural subjects with make
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: A singular subject takes 'makes', and a plural subject takes 'make'.

questions.q: Correct the mistake: *These new rules make every student feels unhappy.*
options: These new rules make every student feel unhappy.
These new rules make every student to feel unhappy.
These new rules makes every student feel unhappy.
These new rules make every student feeling unhappy.
questions.topic: Bare infinitive after make (no -s on the second verb)
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: The verb after 'make + object' stays in the bare infinitive: feel, not feels.

questions.q: Which word completes both sentences? *Yesterday, the sad film ____ me cry.* / *Yesterday, the sad film ____ me sad.*
options: made in the first, make in the second
questions.topic: Past form of make before a verb and an adjective
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: 'Yesterday' needs the past form 'made' before both a bare infinitive (cry) and an adjective (sad).

questions.q: Join the two sentences into one sentence: *The heavy rain fell all night. We felt cold.*
options: The heavy rain made us feel cold.
The heavy rain made us to feel cold.
The heavy rain makes us feel cold.
The heavy rain made us felt cold.
questions.topic: Joining sentences with make + object + infinitive
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: We use the past 'made' + object + bare infinitive: The heavy rain made us feel cold.

questions.q: Change into a yes/no question: *Long school days make students tired.*
options: Do long school days make students tired?
Does long school days make students tired?
Do long school days makes students tired?
Are long school days make students tired?
questions.topic: Making a yes/no question with make
questions.lesson: Causative 'make' | الفعل السببي make (يجعل)
questions.why: The plural subject takes 'Do' and the base form 'make': Do long school days make students tired?

Language review 4 › Making recommendatio.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct form: *You ____ more water in hot weather.*
questions.topic: should + bare infinitive
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: After should we use the verb in the base form, with no to and no -ing.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct form: *Why not ____ a break? You have been working all morning.*
questions.topic: Why not + bare infinitive
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: Why not is a suggestion form and is followed by the bare infinitive, so 'Why not take'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with the correct form: *How about ____ to the beach this Friday?*
questions.topic: How about + verb-ing
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: How about is followed by a verb + -ing, so 'How about going'.

questions.q: Which of these sentences gives a recommendation?
options: You should revise your notes before the exam.
I revised my notes before the exam.
The exam was difficult last year.
She is revising her notes at the moment.
questions.topic: recognising a recommendation
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: Only 'You should revise...' advises the listener; the other three just give facts.

questions.q: Look at this recommendation: *You should visit the old market; it is full of beautiful handcrafts.* Why does the speaker add the second part?
options: To make the advice more convincing
To turn the advice into a question
To show the advice is only for the speaker
To change the verb after should into a gerund
questions.topic: reason after a recommendation
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: The lesson says it is important to give the reason after the advice so that it is convincing.

questions.q: What is the difference in meaning between *You should rest tonight* and *You must rest tonight*?
options: must gives stronger advice than should
should gives stronger advice than must
must is only the question form of should
should can only be used with the pronoun you
questions.topic: should vs must in advice
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: Both give advice, but the lesson lists must as a strong piece of advice.

questions.q: Choose the sentence that is NOT correct.
options: I recommend to visit the new library.
I recommend visiting the new library.
How about visiting the new library?
Why not visit the new library?
questions.topic: I recommend + verb-ing
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: I recommend takes verb + -ing, so 'I recommend to visit' is wrong.

questions.q: Which two forms are followed by a verb + -ing?
options: Why don't you and You must
questions.topic: forms followed by verb-ing
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: In the lesson, How about and I recommend are the two forms followed by the -ing form.

questions.q: Combine the two sentences into one recommendation with a reason: *Visit the National Museum. It has old coins from Yemen.*
options: You should visit the National Museum. It has old coins from Yemen.
You should to visit the National Museum. It has old coins from Yemen.
You should visiting the National Museum. It has old coins from Yemen.
You should visited the National Museum. It has old coins from Yemen.
questions.topic: combining advice with a reason
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: The advice uses should + bare infinitive, and the second sentence gives the reason.

questions.q: Rewrite this sentence as a suggestion with 'Why not': *I think you should try the new juice bar near the school.*
options: Why not try the new juice bar near the school?
Why not to try the new juice bar near the school?
Why not trying the new juice bar near the school?
Why not you try the new juice bar near the school?
questions.topic: rewriting should as Why not
questions.lesson: Making recommendations | تقديم النصائح والاقتراحات (should / Why not ...?)
questions.why: Why not + bare infinitive turns 'I think you should try...' into a suggestion, so 'Why not try...'.
